title: Rosuvastatin -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Rosuvastatin is a lipid-lowering medication belonging to the statin class that inhibits 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis. By decreasing hepatic cholesterol production and upregulating low-density lipoprotein receptors, rosuvastatin effectively reduces circulating low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and total cholesterol levels, thereby lowering the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. The medication has demonstrated efficacy in both primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction and stroke. Rosuvastatin is administered orally and is available in multiple dosage strengths to accommodate individualized treatment goals based on lipid profiles, comorbidities, and overall cardiovascular risk. Monitoring parameters include lipid panels, hepatic function, and creatine kinase levels in select cases. Adverse effects such as myalgia, elevated liver enzymes, and rare instances of rhabdomyolysis necessitate clinician vigilance. Rosuvastatin therapy remains a cornerstone in dyslipidemia management, contributing significantly to the reduction of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.

title: Rosuvastatin -- Continuing Education Activity
content: After participating in this activity, learners gain enhanced competence in the clinical use of rosuvastatin for managing dyslipidemia and reducing cardiovascular risk. The activity strengthens understanding of pharmacologic mechanisms, dosing strategies, and monitoring parameters while emphasizing the importance of individualized, evidence-based care. Clinicians develop the ability to identify and manage adverse drug reactions, optimize therapy in special populations, and recognize drug-drug interactions that may influence safety or efficacy. Collaboration with an interprofessional team, including pharmacists, nurses, and cardiology specialists, enhances patient outcomes through coordinated medication management, timely monitoring, and effective patient education. Pharmacists assist in preventing and resolving drug interactions, nurses contribute to ongoing assessment and adherence support, and clinicians integrate these inputs into patient-centered care plans. This interprofessional approach promotes continuity of care, reduces adverse events, and enhances long-term cardiovascular health for patients undergoing rosuvastatin therapy.

title: Rosuvastatin -- Indications
content: Rosuvastatin is a lipid-lowering statin medication classified as a moderate- to high-intensity statin based on its efficacy in reducing low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels. [1]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Indications -- Food and Drug Administration–Approved Indications
content: Food and Drug Administration (FDA)–approved indications include homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, hyperlipidemia, mixed dyslipidemia, primary dysbetalipoproteinemia, and hypertriglyceridemia. Rosuvastatin is also approved for the primary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. The FDA has approved this medication to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, including nonfatal stroke, cardiovascular death, arterial revascularization, and nonfatal myocardial infarction, in adults without confirmed coronary heart disease who are at higher risk of cardiovascular disease based on age, elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (≥2 mg/L), and at least 1 additional cardiovascular risk factor. [2] [3] The American College of Cardiology (ACC) and the American Heart Association (AHA) endorse moderate- to high-intensity statin therapy for reducing the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), depending on LDL reduction goals. In 2025, a guideline published by the ACC, the AHA, the American College of Emergency Physicians, the National Association of Emergency Medicine Physicians, and the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions recommended initiating high-intensity statin therapy in all patients with acute coronary syndrome. Moderate-intensity statin therapy is indicated for adults aged 40 to 75 with diabetes mellitus, regardless of estimated 10-year ASCVD risk. [4] [5] [6]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Indications -- Off-Label Uses
content: Off-label uses include noncardioembolic stroke, secondary prevention of transient ischemic attack, and perioperative cardiac risk reduction in patients undergoing noncardiac surgeries. Rosuvastatin is also beneficial in acute ischemic stroke. [7] According to results from a meta-analysis, statin therapy significantly reduces mortality in heart transplant recipients and decreases the incidence of fatal rejection and coronary vasculopathy. Further prospective studies are needed to validate these outcomes. [8] [9] [10]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Mechanism of Action
content: The mechanism of action of rosuvastatin is the inhibition of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the rate-limiting step in cholesterol synthesis. Inhibition of this enzyme reduces the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonic acid, thereby increasing the number of low-density lipoprotein receptors on hepatocyte membranes and stimulating the catabolism of low-density lipoprotein. HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors also decrease the levels of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and exhibit pleiotropic effects, including inhibition of platelet aggregation, anticoagulant activity, reduction of vascular inflammation, and enhancement of endothelial function. [11] [12]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Mechanism of Action -- Pharmacokinetics
content: Absorption: Peak plasma concentrations of rosuvastatin occur 3 to 5 hours following oral administration. The absolute bioavailability of rosuvastatin is approximately 20%. The area under the concentration-time curve of rosuvastatin is unaffected by food intake or the time of administration. Distribution: The mean volume of distribution is approximately 134 L. Rosuvastatin has a plasma protein binding of 88%, primarily to albumin.

title: Rosuvastatin -- Mechanism of Action -- Pharmacokinetics
content: Metabolism : Hepatic uptake is mediated by organic anion-transporting polypeptides (OATPs), particularly OATP1B1 and OATP1B3. [13] [14] The efflux transporter breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP) also modulates the absorption and disposition of rosuvastatin. [15] Rosuvastatin undergoes minimal metabolism by the cytochrome P450 2C9 enzyme. [16]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Mechanism of Action -- Pharmacokinetics
content: Excretion : Rosuvastatin is a hydrophilic compound with an elimination half-life of approximately 19 hours, primarily excreted into the bile and subsequently into the feces (approximately 90%). Only around 10% is eliminated in the urine. [17] [18]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Administration -- Available Dosage Forms and Strengths
content: Rosuvastatin is available in tablet and capsule formulations. The tablet can be administered orally, with or without food, or via a nasogastric tube. The medication may be taken at any time of the day and should be swallowed whole. The capsule should not be crushed or chewed. If opened, the capsule contents should be emptied into 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of applesauce and swallowed immediately without chewing.

title: Rosuvastatin -- Administration -- Available Dosage Forms and Strengths
content: For administration via a nasogastric tube, the capsule may be opened and its contents transferred into a 60-mL catheter-tipped syringe. The recommendation is to add 40 mL of water, replace the plunger, and shake for 15 seconds. The syringe should be attached to a nasogastric tube of at least 16 French gauge. The medication is then administered, followed by flushing the tube with 20 mL of water. The mixture should be administered immediately after preparation. Tablet strengths available for both generic and brand formulations include 5, 10, 20, and 40 mg.

title: Rosuvastatin -- Administration -- Adult Dosage
content: Dosing is individualized based on baseline LDL-C levels and the therapeutic goal. Therapeutic response and adherence are essential determinants of therapeutic success. Dosage adjustments should occur at intervals of 4 weeks or more, depending on the indication and whether primary or secondary prevention is the goal.

title: Rosuvastatin -- Administration -- Adult Dosage
content: High-intensity rosuvastatin therapy is 20 to 40 mg once daily, achieving an LDL-C reduction of 50% or greater. Moderate-intensity rosuvastatin therapy: 5 mg to 10 mg daily, achieving an LDL-C reduction of 30% to 49%. [19] [20] Due to the risk of significant drug-drug interactions, the dose adjustment should be performed in consultation with a pharmacist.

title: Rosuvastatin -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Hepatic impairment: Increased serum transaminase levels and cases of fatal and nonfatal hepatic failure have been reported. Baseline liver function tests should be obtained before initiating therapy and periodically thereafter.  If clinically significant hepatic injury with hyperbilirubinemia or jaundice occurs,  rosuvastatin should be discontinued immediately. [16]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Renal impairment: If the creatinine clearance is greater than 30 mL/min, no dosage adjustment is necessary. However, if the clearance is less than 30 mL/min, therapy should be initiated at 5 mg once daily, with a maximum of 10 mg daily. The Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes guidelines recommend statin or statin/ezetimibe therapy for adults aged 50 or older with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m², who are not receiving chronic dialysis or kidney transplantation. [21]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Pregnancy considerations: Because rosuvastatin and other statin medications reduce the synthesis of cholesterol and other biologically active substances derived from cholesterol, fetal harm may occur when administered during pregnancy.  The 2018 AHA/ACC guidelines recommend that women of childbearing age who are sexually active use reliable contraception while taking a statin medication. Women planning pregnancy should discontinue statin medications 1 to 2 months before conception or immediately upon recognizing pregnancy to avoid fetal exposure. [20]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Breastfeeding considerations: Although levels of rosuvastatin in breast milk are minimal, limited data indicate the potential for effects on the infant. Because statin therapy reduces cholesterol synthesis and may cause adverse effects, breastfeeding is generally not recommended during treatment. Current guidelines advise avoiding breastfeeding due to potential disruptions in infant lipid metabolism. However, some experts note that children with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia starting statins at 1 year of age have a low risk of complications, particularly with rosuvastatin or pravastatin. Until additional data are available, alternative treatments such as bile acid sequestrants may be preferable. [22]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Children: For children with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, the recommended dose of rosuvastatin is 5 to 10 mg daily for children aged 8 to 10 and 5 to 20 mg daily for those older than 10. For homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, the recommended dose of rosuvastatin is 20 mg daily for children aged 7 or older. The safety and effectiveness of rosuvastatin have not been established in children younger than 8 with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, or those younger than 7 with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.

title: Rosuvastatin -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Older adults: The American Geriatrics Society/National Lipid Association joint guidelines emphasize that ASCVD risk increases with age, and elevated LDL-C and non–high-density lipoprotein cholesterol remain predictive in adults aged 75 or older. Risk assessment is challenging because most risk calculators do not account for comorbidities, frailty, or cognitive impairment. Shared decision-making and a patient-centered approach are essential for primary prevention, and coronary artery calcium scoring helps guide these decisions. Withholding therapy may be reasonable if the coronary artery calcium score is 0. The AHA/ACC notes that initiating a moderate-intensity statin may be reasonable in adults aged 75 or older with LDL-C levels of 70 to 189 mg/dL (1.7-4.8 mmol/L). LDL-C should be monitored every 3 to 12 months. Deprescribing may be considered, and ezetimibe or bempedoic acid may be used if LDL-C levels remain above target or in cases of statin intolerance. [6] [23]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Asian individuals: According to product labeling, rosuvastatin should be initiated at 5 mg once daily in Asian individuals due to the potential for increased plasma concentrations. Rosuvastatin exposure is approximately 2-fold higher in Asian individuals compared to White individuals. Therefore, the risks and benefits should be carefully considered, and the dose adjusted if doses greater than 20 mg once daily are not effective.

content: Some studies suggest that genetic variations in 2 specific proteins, solute carrier organic anion transporter family member 1B1 ( SLCO1B1 ), which encodes OATP1B1, and ATP-binding cassette subfamily G member 2 ( ABCG2) , which encodes BCRP, are more reliable predictors of rosuvastatin exposure than ethnicity alone. [24]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Adverse Effects -- Clinically Relevant Adverse Effects
content: Clinically significant adverse effects of rosuvastatin include the following: Creatinine kinase of >10 times the upper limit of normal Severe myopathy Rhabdomyolysis Aspartate aminotransferase or alanine aminotransferase elevations of >3 times the upper limit of normal Statin-induced acute kidney injury [25] [26] [27]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Adverse Effects -- Clinically Relevant Adverse Effects
content: Rare adverse effects include new-onset diabetes mellitus, hematuria, proteinuria, and hypersensitivity reactions. [28] Other reported adverse effects include headache, dizziness, nausea, constipation, interstitial cystitis, arthralgia, and weakness.

title: Rosuvastatin -- Adverse Effects -- Drug-Drug Interactions (Table 2)
content: Medications that may increase the risk of myopathy when coadministered with rosuvastatin: Fibrates, colchicine, daptomycin, fusidic acid, niacin, niacinamide, raltegravir, red yeast rice extract, and rupatadine. Medications that may decrease the serum concentration of rosuvastatin: Antacids, apalutamide, elagolix, and eslicarbazepine. Medications that may increase the serum concentrations of rosuvastatin: Clopidogrel, cobicistat, cyclosporine, daclatasvir, dasabuvir, dronedarone, elbasvir, eltrombopag, eluxadoline, fostamatinib, glecaprevir, pibrentasvir, grazoprevir, itraconazole, ledipasvir, letermovir, ombitasvir, paritaprevir, ritonavir, osimertinib, protease inhibitors, simeprevir, teriflunomide, velpatasvir, and voxilaprevir.

title: Rosuvastatin -- Contraindications
content: Rosuvastatin or any component of the drug formulation is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity. Other contraindications, as per the FDA-approved label, include acute liver failure, decompensated cirrhosis, and unexplained persistent elevations of serum transaminases. [29] [30] Statin medications should be avoided in pregnancy, but may be considered in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. Bile acid sequestrants are preferred alternatives in pregnancy. [31] Notably, the FDA has removed pregnancy from its list of contraindications for statin use.[ U.S. Food & Drug Administration. Statins: Drug Safety Communication - FDA Requests Removal of Strongest Warning Against Using Cholesterol-lowering Statins During Pregnancy ]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Contraindications -- Warnings and Precautions
content: Diabetes mellitus: Statin medications may increase glycosylated hemoglobin and fasting serum glucose levels, although the incidence of this effect may vary. [32] The ACC/AHA guidelines and other experts state that the cardiovascular risk-reducing benefits of statin therapy outweigh the generally mild rise in serum glucose levels or new-onset diabetes. [33]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Contraindications -- Warnings and Precautions
content: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy: Sporadic reports of this autoimmune condition have been associated with statin use, including recurrence after the same or a different statin. Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy is characterized by proximal muscle weakness and increased serum creatine kinase levels that persist despite the discontinuation of statin therapy. Characteristic features include positive anti–HMG-CoA reductase antibodies and muscle biopsy findings of necrotizing myopathy. Further neuromuscular and serologic evaluations may be required. Treatment with immunosuppressive agents may be necessary; in such cases, rosuvastatin should be discontinued if immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy is suspected. [34] [35]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Contraindications -- Warnings and Precautions
content: Statin-associated muscle symptoms: According to the National Lipid Association guidelines, this term encompasses myalgia, myopathy, myonecrosis, and rhabdomyolysis. [36] [37] Proximal, symmetric muscle weakness or soreness is a typical presentation of myopathy: Myalgia: Muscle aches, muscle soreness, and muscle stiffness, with normal creatine kinase levels. Myopathy: Muscle weakness, not necessarily associated with elevated creatine kinase levels. Myonecrosis: Muscle enzyme elevations (creatine kinase) or hyperkalemia. Rhabdomolysis: Severe condition associated with myonecrosis, myoglobinuria, and acute kidney injury. [38]

[36] [37] Proximal, symmetric muscle weakness or soreness is a typical presentation of myopathy: Myalgia: Muscle aches, muscle soreness, and muscle stiffness, with normal creatine kinase levels. Myopathy: Muscle weakness, not necessarily associated with elevated creatine kinase levels. Myonecrosis: Muscle enzyme elevations (creatine kinase) or hyperkalemia. Rhabdomolysis: Severe condition associated with myonecrosis, myoglobinuria, and acute kidney injury. [38]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Monitoring
content: Lipid panel testing, including LDL-C, high-density lipoprotein, triglycerides, and total cholesterol, should be obtained at the initial visit to establish a baseline for future monitoring and treatment. Thereafter, a fasting lipid profile should be obtained within 4 to 12 weeks of initiation or a dose adjustment. Furthermore, fasting lipid profiles should be obtained every 3 to 12 months or as clinically indicated. If 2 consecutive low-density lipoprotein levels are less than 40 mg/d, the dose should be decreased.

title: Rosuvastatin -- Toxicity -- Signs and Symptoms of Overdose
content: Rhabdomyolysis is the most clinically significant toxic adverse effect of rosuvastatin. If severe muscle symptoms or fatigue occur, the medication should be discontinued, and creatine phosphokinase, serum creatinine, and urinalysis should be obtained to evaluate for myoglobinuria. If mild-to-moderate muscle symptoms are present, the drug should be discontinued to assess for other causes of myalgia. [42] Switching to a different statin medication at a lower dose may relieve muscle symptoms. Statin medications inhibit the HMG-CoA pathway, which can hinder coenzyme Q10 production and disrupt cellular energy production, leading to muscle cell death. [43]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Toxicity -- Management of Overdose
content: No antidotes are available for rosuvastatin overdose. Patients should be provided with supportive care. If the underlying etiology is resolved, patients can restart the original rosuvastatin dose or a lower dose; however, if symptoms recur, rosuvastatin should be discontinued indefinitely. title: Rosuvastatin -- Toxicity -- Management of Overdose
content: Prompt discontinuation of the statin medication. Initiation of aggressive intravenous hydration to prevent acute kidney injury. Correction of electrolyte disturbances: If hyperkalemia (potassium >6 mmol/L) and electrocardiogram changes are present, intravenous calcium gluconate should be administered. Additionally, insulin-dextrose and nebulized albuterol are recommended to shift potassium intracellularly. The concomitant use of fibrates should be avoided. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate should be used in severe acidosis. [44] Hemodialysis may be required for patients who do not improve with intravenous fluids, electrolyte correction, and urine alkalinization. [45] If statin-associated immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy develops, corticosteroids, rituximab, methotrexate, and intravenous immunoglobulin are used. [46] In severe cases, consultation with the local poison control center or a medical toxicologist is advised for the most current management recommendations. [47]

title: Rosuvastatin -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Rosuvastatin is a widely used lipid-lowering medication and is effective in preventing cardiovascular disease. [48] Treatment with this medication requires interprofessional collaboration and communication among clinicians, pharmacists, nurses, and other subspecialties, such as cardiologists, who may assist in dose titration and ongoing management. Because rosuvastatin has multiple drug-drug interactions, pharmacists should evaluate for any interactions and notify the clinician. Pharmacists play a crucial role in managing statin-gemfibrozil and statin-niacin interactions using standardized protocols. Their interventions safely resolve interactions with minimal impact on triglyceride levels, while improving care efficiency. [49] Nurses monitor for adverse reactions, assess therapeutic effectiveness, educate patients, and serve as a liaison for other team members. Clinicians should determine the risks and benefits of the medication during shared decision-making with patients, following an informed consent discussion. An interprofessional team approach among clinicians, specialists, pharmacists, and nurses is crucial to reducing adverse effects, improving disease course and quality of life, and improving patient outcomes related to rosuvastatin therapy.
